name: ia-operation
thesis: Make the first level of Forge the consequence the operator is about to have on production - Home, Research, Deliver, Studio, Content Admin, Settings - because the consequence class is the only axis Forge can derive mechanically from the work in front of it and prove from its own state, and because it is the axis on which the workload actually splits: reads are frequent, cheap and should confirm nothing; package runs are frequent, irreversible and should confirm once with the counts restated; publishing is rare, the most consequential thing in the product, and deserves its own destination, colour family and authority; and recovery is a phase of a job, so it belongs beside the pause that caused it rather than in a destination of its own. Content type stays as the second axis - lanes on the Command Center and filters inside each destination - because 15 of the 41 committed manifests carry reads and writes together and one carries two entity types, so a content-first first level cannot hold a real package.

navigation_model.name: Consequence-first operations shell (operation-oriented, lanes as the second axis)
navigation_model.description: The first level is what the operator is about to do to production, because that is the one axis Forge can derive mechanically from the work in front of it and prove from its own state: Home, Research (reads), Deliver (packages, jobs and recovery), Studio (authoring and projects, zero live footprint), Content Admin (records, review and publish) and Settings. Content type is the second axis: lanes on the Command Center and filters inside Research, Deliver and Admin, never a destination that owns work, because 15 of 41 committed manifests carry both reads and writes and one carries two entity types. The approved shell is unchanged - Command Center home, a persistent 232px rail on desktop, five bottom items plus a More sheet on the phone, visual lanes, a first-class Content Admin - and the approved operation-mode header becomes the mechanism that carries the create/update/upload/capture distinction inside a destination rather than splitting it across destinations. Reads are the cheapest path and confirm nothing; writes confirm once per job with the counts restated; publishing gets its own destination, its own colour family and its own confirmation; recovery is a state of the job that needs it, rendered where the pause happened.

authority_lanes.principle: One product, two authorities. Content Operations acts on PACKAGES and JOBS; Content Admin acts on RECORDS. The two lanes share the runner, the journal and the safety invariants, and share nothing in their vocabulary.
structural_separation: Separate top-level destination with its own second level; no admin screen is reachable from a Deliver screen and no Deliver screen is reachable from an admin screen except through the rail/bottom nav.
The admin lane renders no manifest text, no procedure path, no journal state, no item pill, no budget row, no capture key, no orphan card. Those live only under Deliver and Research.

Pill families are disjoint and this is the primary structural cue: the admin lane uses ONLY the content pills HIDDEN / DRAFT / PUBLISHED (plus SENT - UNCONFIRMED while a publish is in flight); the operator lane uses the job and item pills PLANNED / SENT / CONFIRMED / VERIFIED / FAILED / ORPHANED / SKIPPED / PAUSED / INCOMPLETE / RUNNING / DONE / ABORTED.

An admin action is still journaled and still read back; it is PRESENTED as a record result ('saved and read back at 14:02'), not as a job. The write-ahead journal, the SENT reconciliation and the read-back are preserved unchanged below the presentation seam.

Role is read once per session through profile.getPublicUser (one public budget unit) or profile.getUser, held in memory only, never persisted, never a cookie or token read. Without a canChangeContent role the destination is a labelled placeholder, never a hidden row.
visual_separation: Gold (--pub, --pub-text) is the admin/review/publish family and appears nowhere in the operator lane except the PUBLISHED content pill.

Crimson (--mut) is the operator live-write family and appears nowhere in the admin lane: the admin never sees a LIVE WRITE band. An admin edit arms its own confirmation in the neutral/write construction only at the moment of send.

The admin lane carries no ModeBand while reading; a PUBLISH band appears only on the publish sheet and on the record while a publish is in flight. This is a deliberate reduction of the approved mode-header rule and is listed as a departure for the director.
Geometry: the three production ink buttons (Start live write, Publish, Reconcile & resume) are the only 0-radius controls in the app, so 'square means it touches production' holds in both lanes.
how_data_moves: 1. The operator runs a package in Deliver. Hidden records are created or updated; the journal records entityId, manifestPath and manifestHash per item; the results bundle is committed to harvests/inbox (app.mjs:369-406).

2. Forge writes a repository-backed REVIEW handoff naming the package, the records by id and class, and the operator who staged them. The durable home is the repository, not Forge: the existing roadmap task status REVIEW (scripts/content_workstream.py:59) plus a per-package review record. Exactly where and in what shape is K-09/K-47 and is not settled here.

3. The admin queue reads that repository-backed state from the GitHub listing cache (no game request), then resolves each entry to its live record by a point read when the entry is opened, not when the queue is listed.
4. The admin decides. An edit is a whole-record fetch-merge update; a publish is the same update with the lifecycle field flipped. Both go through the runner and the journal.

5. The disposition (approved / changes requested / published, with the read-back verdict and the record ids) is written back to the same repository-backed record, so the operator sees it in the Project workspace and in the package's last-run tag. Nothing about approval is claimed to be live game state.
6. Nothing in this loop invents a second canonical content database: the game owns the records, the repository owns the review state, Forge owns neither.

the_mix: Reads dominate. 42 committed bundles, 21 of 41 manifests capture-only, and the top capture procedures are quests.get (150 manifest captures), ai.getAiProfile (28), profile.getAi (26), gameAsset.get (23), jutsu.get (16).
Writes are frequent but concentrated in one shape. 148 write items: 113 quest:edit, 26 asset:create, 8 ai:edit, 1 jutsu:create, and zero quest:create.
Reads and writes travel together. 15 of 41 manifests carry both write items and captures (14 json plus the 31-quest icon-swap pack), because capture.after IS the read-back.
Entity mixing inside one package is rare but real: 34 of 35 json manifests are single-entity, and one zip pack (21_bg_assets_and_wiring) carries 8 asset:create plus 10 quest:edit in 18 items.
Publishing is the rarest and the most consequential: three archived publish/hide manifests and 26 hidden-flag edits in one bundle, every one of them a user tap on Builder under skipPreflight.

Recovery is rare but real and expensive: 9 UNVERIFIED junk jutsu from one entity misroute, one poisoned idmap key that rode along in every later bundle, and one server-side objective-field drop that only the whole-record diff caught.
why_operation_first: The consequence class is the one axis Forge can DERIVE mechanically and prove. read-only is already computed from an empty plan (screens.mjs:120); creates/updates/uploads/captures all come from the parsed plan and the manifest capture arrays. A content-type axis cannot be derived for a package that carries two entity types, and no axis at all can be derived for the 15 packages that mix reads and writes.

The approved mode header only makes sense inside an operation-first IA. If the first level were content type, the operator would choose 'Quests' and only then learn that this particular quest package writes 31 live records. Operation-first puts the consequence in the destination and the counts in the band.

The frequency and the risk point in opposite directions, which is exactly what an operation axis expresses: the most frequent action (read) gets the shallowest path and zero confirmations, and the rarest action (publish) gets its own destination, its own colour family and its own confirmation.

The three shapes that keep Builder installed (capture bodies for generator scripts, paged list captures, procedures outside the registry) are all READS. An operation-first IA gives them one destination with one honest capability statement, instead of scattering 'this read is not supported yet' across six content lanes.

Recovery is a phase of a job, not a place. Today it is split across Jobs and Run and that is a real, catalogued defect; an operation-first Deliver destination that holds packages, jobs and the recovery decision together repairs it rather than institutionalising it.
frequency_and_risk_rationale.what_the_lanes_are_for: Content lanes survive as the approved entry principle, but as the SECOND axis: a lane is a filter and a starting point on the Command Center, not a destination that owns work. Tapping the Quests & Events lane opens Research or Deliver already filtered, or opens Quest Studio; it never opens a place where a mixed package cannot be shown.

weaknesses: The strongest anti-content-type argument is weaker than it first looks. 34 of the 35 committed json manifests are single-entity; only one zip pack mixes entity types. A content-type-first IA can therefore classify almost every real package correctly, and its advocates can cite that directly. My case rests on the read/write mix (15 of 41) and on derivability, not on entity mixing.

A package can move between Research and Deliver when its plan changes, because the classification is derived. An operator who learned 'the census manifest lives in Research' will find a later revision of it in Deliver. Mitigations (one search across both, a mode chip on every row) reduce but do not remove the surprise.

'Research' and 'Deliver' are vocabulary the operator has to learn; 'Quests' and 'Items' are vocabulary they already have. The migration cost of an operation axis falls entirely on the one person who uses the tool daily.

The Research destination ships partly empty. The three shapes that keep Builder installed (generator-fed capture bodies, paged list captures, procedures outside the registry) are all reads, so until G-02 and G-03 pass, the destination built around reads is the one with the most disabled controls. That is honest but it reads as a broken destination, and it is a real first-impression risk.

Deliver and Content Admin both need record reads, and every draft-queue read is publicProcedure on a 60/60s window shared with the carrier page. Two destinations that each hold a read cache can double-spend the budget. The design needs one shared cache policy and an explicit refresh, which I specify but do not prove.

Studio as a first-level destination is thin today: the code exists only on a ChatGPT branch, holds one draft per device keyed by the device clock, supports only Mission, and ends at a text export because no promotion contract exists. A destination whose primary journey terminates in a copy/paste is a weak destination until K-39 is ruled.

Presenting an admin publish as a record result while journaling it as a single-item job is an architectural claim, not a proven pattern. It depends on K-08 (staged package versus direct hidden-record edit) and on a publish recipe that does not exist; if the director rules for staged packages, the admin lane gains a package concept and my 'the admin never sees a manifest' promise needs re-examination.

Lanes lose their place in the navigation. They live only on the Command Center, which is weaker than the mockup implies and weaker than a two-axis IA would give them. If the director wants lane-first browsing as a primary path, the two-axis family serves that better than this one.

The tap counts assume the package is already committed to push/ on main. Every count I give excludes the repository session that authored the manifest, which is where most of the real elapsed time goes; an IA change cannot improve that.

I reduce the approved operation-mode band on the admin surface (DEP-6). If the director rules that the band must be persistent everywhere, the 'intentionally simpler' character of Content Admin weakens and the phone chrome budget on admin screens rises by 44px.
